blocks.text: When we place an element of area in an electric field, some of the lines of force pass through it (Fig. 9.10). The number of the field lines passing through a certain element of area is known as electric flux through that area. It is usually denoted by Greek letter φₑ. For example, the electric flux φₑ through the area A in Fig 9.10 is 4 while the flux through B is 2.

blocks.alt: Magenta field lines run upward and spread apart. Near the bottom, where they are close together, a small yellow area A is crossed by 4 lines. Higher up, where they are farther apart, an equal yellow area B is crossed by 2 lines.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.10: Electric flux through a surface normal to E (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.10).

blocks.text: In order to give a quantitative meaning to flux, the field lines are drawn such that the number of field lines passing through a unit area held perpendicular to field lines at a point represent the intensity E of the field at that point.
Usually, the element of area is represented by a vector area A whose magnitude is equal to the surface area A of the element and whose direction is along normal to the area.

Electric Flux Through a Surface Enclosing a Charge

Let us calculate the electric flux through a closed surface, in shape of a sphere of radius r due to a point charge q placed at the centre of sphere as shown in Fig. 9.12. To apply the formula φₑ = E.A for the computation of electric flux, the surface area should be flat. For this reason the total surface area of the sphere is divided into n small patches with areas of magnitudes ΔA₁, ΔA₂, ΔA₃, ……, ΔAₙ respectively as shown in Fig. 9.12. The direction of each vector area is along perpendicular drawn outward to the corresponding patch. The electric intensities at the centres of vector areas ΔA₁, ΔA₂, ΔA₃, ……, ΔAₙ are E₁, E₂, E₃, ……, Eₙ respectively.

blocks.alt: A large shaded sphere with a charge +q at its centre. On a small curved patch Delta A of its surface a black arrow Delta A and a red arrow E both point radially outward.

blocks.text: Now Imagine that a closed surface S is enclosing this sphere. It can be seen in Fig 9.13 that the flux through the closed surface S is the same as that through the sphere. So, we can conclude that total flux through a closed surface does not depend upon the shape or geometry of the closed surface. It depends upon the medium and the charge enclosed.
